title: Flight booking requirements
idea: Scoping a flight booking system means naming its actors and use cases, separating fare inventory from seat choice, and saying what v1 leaves out.
points: Travellers search flights, hold a fare, add passengers, pay, and get tickets.
A fare class sells a count of seats; seat numbers are chosen separately.
Core rule: fare counts in a cabin never add up past its seats.
Assume heavy search traffic and few bookings; state these numbers as assumptions.

edges.caption: The traveller searches by origin, destination and date. We assume this is the busiest use case.
Picking a flight and fare class holds that many seats in the fare's count.
The traveller enters each passenger's name and travel document while the hold lasts.
Payment confirms the booking, and the system issues one ticket per passenger.

edges.label: then
edges.caption: Seat numbers are picked after the fare is secured. A booking is valid without them.

edges.label: expires
edges.caption: The system releases holds that pass their time limit, returning seats to the fare class.
Multi-city trips, loyalty miles and deliberate overbooking wait for later. Say so early.

code.title: Use cases per actor
code.caption: The scope as code: each use case belongs to one actor, and v1 is an explicit set.

walk.text: v1 is a named set; anything missing from it is deferred by default.
Group use cases under their actor and tag each IN or OUT.
Print the size of the cut so the scope discussion has a number.
Three actors: the traveller, airline operations, and the system itself.
Six traveller use cases form the booking path, seat choice included.
Multi-city, miles, scheduling and overbooking are listed so the cut is visible.

pitfalls: Do not merge fare inventory and seat numbers; travellers often book before choosing seats.
State traffic and hold length as assumptions, not as facts about real airlines.
Leaving the system actor out hides hold expiry until late in the design.

quiz.q: An interviewer asks for overbooking in v1. What is the best scoping reply?
options: Add it now; every airline needs it on day one
Drop the capacity rule so overbooking happens on its own
Allow it only for business class
Defer it; keep the capacity rule strict in v1
quiz.why: Overbooking is a deliberate business policy on top of a strict capacity rule. Build the strict rule first; a later policy can raise the limit.

takeaway: Agree on actors, use cases and the capacity rule before drawing classes.

starters: Why do airlines sell fare classes instead of specific seats?
How long should a fare hold last in this design?
How would overbooking change the requirements later?
